claims.text: The name humppa was invented by Antero Alpola for a radio show in the 1950s.
Humppa is related to jazz and fast foxtrot, played two beats to a bar.
The band probably used a tuba, as the sound of tuba on the first beat is like hump, the second beat coming as a pa.
One form of Humppa dance is related to one-step, which arrived in Finland 1913.
The second Humppa form is related to two-step, which came to Finland in 1910.
A third form of dance, Nilkku, is based on a slow, slow, quick, quick rhythm.
The revival meant that humppa had become the most popular music and dancing form for older people and for the countryside's youth in the Eastern and South-Eastern parts of the country.

sections.origins_and_history: The fatele originated as a traditional dance-song in Tuvalu. It faced suppression in the 1860s due to missionary influence but evolved in the 20th century, incorporating elements of the Samoan siva dance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Traditionally performed sitting or kneeling by women. Modern performances feature women standing in lines, enacting stories through arm and body movements while men provide rhythmic accompaniment.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features singing led by older men in a meeting hall (maneapa). Percussion is provided by beating hands on mats, empty cabin cracker cans, or wooden tea chests.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear titi fakamanumanu (coconut leaf skirts), titi kaulama (layered skirts), teuga saka (tops), and various floral garlands and bands. Performances occur in community spaces like the maneapa.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at weddings, church festivals, and to honor prominent visitors. It is a competitive tradition that serves as a community celebration.
sections.notable_figures: Gerd Koch (anthropologist who recorded traditional songs in 1960-1961).
sections.regional_variants: Shared tradition between Tuvalu and Tokelau.
sections.lineage: Influenced by Samoan siva dance and European melody and harmony.

sections.origins_and_history: Western swing arose in the late 1920s and early 1930s out of house parties, ranch dances, and small-town dance halls across Texas and Oklahoma. Pioneers like Bob Wills, Milton Brown, and the Light Crust Doughboys blended traditional fiddle tunes with jazz and blues. By the late 1930s and 1940s, the style achieved massive popularity, broadcasting via powerful radio stations like KVOO and packing ballrooms across the Southwest and California.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers engaged in simple couples dances, including two-steps and the Lindy Hop, enhanced with Western twirls. By 1937, the jitterbug gained immense popularity in the West, characterized by a style that was smoother and more subdued than the all-out boogie woogie.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is performed by a hot string band featuring fiddles, mandolin, upright bass, electric and acoustic guitars, and banjos, frequently augmented by drums, saxophones, trumpets, trombones, pianos, accordion, and the distinctive electrically amplified steel guitar.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers gathered in expansive ballrooms, dance pavilions, and nightspots such as Cain's Ballroom in Tulsa, the Crystal Springs Dance Pavilion in Fort Worth, and the Venice Pier Ballroom in California, often drawing thousands of attendees on Saturday nights.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Saturday night dances served as the core of social life for working-class communities throughout Texas, Oklahoma, and California, providing a vital recreational outlet amid the hardships of the Great Depression and World War II.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Bob Wills, co-founder of the Light Crust Doughboys and leader of the Texas Playboys; Milton Brown, pioneer of Western swing vocal styling; Spade Cooley, bandleader dubbed the 'King of Western Swing'; and Johnnie Lee Wills and Hank Thompson, who carried the tradition forward.
sections.regional_variants: The genre developed distinct regional hubs, originating in the Texas-Oklahoma borderlands and expanding dramatically during World War II into a thriving California scene centered around Los Angeles area ballrooms.
sections.lineage: Western swing developed as an outgrowth of country music and jazz. It subsequently influenced later genres including honky-tonk, rockabilly, and country rock.

sections.origins_and_history: Pungmul is rooted in the dure collective labor farming culture, rural holidays, community-building events, and shamanistic rituals. During the Japanese colonial era (1910–1945), colonial authorities promoted the term nongak to limit its scope and suppress its cultural meaning. In the late 1960s and 1970s, it gained new life in political protests during the pro-democracy movement. In 1978, performers created SamulNori, a seated indoor staging that popularized the tradition globally.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Most performances take place outdoors with dozens of players in constant motion, featuring group formations (jinpuri), solo performances by the lead gong player (Sangsoe Noleum), hat-streamer twirling (Sangmonori), hourglass drum solos (Suljanggu Noleum), small drum dances (Sogo Noleum), and satirical character skits (japsaek).
sections.music_and_instruments: Drumming is the central element of pungmul, utilizing five major instruments: the kkwaenggwari (small handheld gong), janggu (hourglass drum), buk (barrel drum), jing (gong), and sogo (small handle drum). Wind instruments such as the taepyeongso (hojeok, senap, or nalari) also accompany the drummers. Rhythm patterns are known as jangdan.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear colorful costumes, most commonly featuring a flowery version of the Buddhist gokkal head-dress. Advanced troupe members wear sangmo hats with long ribbons spun via knee bends. Settings are traditionally outdoor village streets, fields, and community spaces.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically played during farm work, lunar holidays, village community events, shamanistic rituals, and fundraising. In the late 20th century, it became an important artistic medium for political protest and expression during the pro-democracy movement.
sections.notable_figures: Kim Duk-soo, Kim Yong-bae, Sim U-seong, Kim Swoo Geun, Kim Bong Jun, and Yi Jong-hun.
sections.regional_variants: Recognized in five primary regional styles under South Korean cultural property designation: Jinju Samcheonpo nongak (yeongnam style), Pyeongtaek nongak (utdari style), Iri nongak (honam udo style), Gangneung nongak (yeongdong style), and Imsil Pilbong nongak (honam jwado style, known for rapid rhythms and varying formations).
sections.lineage: Rooted in ancient agricultural and shamanistic traditions; gave rise to modern staged percussion genres like SamulNori and shares historical ties with itinerant Namsadang troupes.

claims.text: Pungmul is a Korean folk music tradition that includes drumming, dancing, and singing.
Pungmul is rooted in the dure (collective labor) farming culture.
Each group is led by a kkwaenggwari small handheld gong player.
Older scholars often describe this tradition as nongak, a term meaning farmers' music whose usage arose during the colonial era.
In an advanced troupe all performers may wear sangmo, which are hats with long ribbon attached to them that players can spin and flip in intricate patterns powered by knee bends.

sections.origins_and_history: The oral tradition places the origins of the morna on Boa Vista Island in the 18th century, potentially evolving from a cross between local working choros and the introduced lundum. By the 19th century, it was a fully formed genre, with compositions like 'Brada Maria' documented around 1870. The 2nd period, led by Eugénio Tavares in the early 20th century on Brava Island, introduced slower tempos and romantic lyricism focused on love and separation. The 3rd period in the 1930s and 1940s saw São Vicente composer B. Leza incorporate Brazilian-influenced passing chords, expanding harmonic possibilities beyond the traditional cycle of fifths. The 4th period (1950s-1970s) coincided with the rise of the coladeira and the incorporation of political and homeland themes. Recent years have seen increased artistic freedom, with contemporary composers experimenting with chord sequences and fusions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: As a dance the morna is a ballroom dance, danced in pairs. The performers dance with an arm embracing the partner, while with the other arm they hold hands. The dancing is made through two body swings to one side in a music's bar, while in the next bar the swinging is to the other side.
sections.music_and_instruments: Characterized by a lento tempo and a 2-beat bar (sometimes 4), traditional morna relies on a harmonic structure based on a cycle of fifths and is almost always monotonic. The melody features frequent syncopation, extending notes from the end of a bar to the strong beat of the next. The primary instrument is the guitar (*violão*), utilizing a specific fingerpicking and strumming technique called *mãozada* that articulates a thumb-driven bass line with arpeggiated or rhythmic chords. Ensembles also incorporate cavaquinhos, ten or twelve-string violas, violins (*rabecas*), pianos, and various percussion instruments.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at key life events such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions. Central themes include universal subjects like love, as well as distinctively Cape Verdean realities: departure abroad, return, saudade, love for the homeland, and the sea.
sections.notable_figures: Cesária Évora, Eugénio Tavares, B. Leza (Francisco Xavier da Cruz), Bana, Celina Pereira, Teté Alhinho, Jorge Monteiro, Manuel de Novas, Ildo Lobo.
sections.regional_variants: Boa Vista morna is the oldest variant, characterized by a quicker tempo (andante ~96 bpm), rubato style, simpler structure, and satirical or social themes. Brava morna features a slower tempo (lento ~60 bpm), strong romanticism, rhymes, and a rigid meter. São Vicente morna shares the slower tempo of Brava but incorporates enriched passing chords, wider non-rigid themes, and lacks strict rhyming.
sections.lineage: Considered by some authors to be a cross between local choros and the lundum. It served as a precursor and contemporary to the coladeira.

claims.text: The morna was proclaimed Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in December 2019.
The dance involves two body swings to one side per bar and two to the other side on the next bar.
Eugénio Tavares introduced romantic lyricism to the morna in the early 20th century.
B. Leza introduced passing chords known as the meio-tom brasileiro in the 1930s and 1940s.

sections.origins_and_history: The Semah is rooted in the Alevi-Bektaşi belief system, which is based on admiration for Ali. It is a living tradition transmitted orally through generations.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform in circular patterns and rotate around their own axes. Men and women dance together. The right palm faces upward and the left palm faces downward.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is played on the 'saz' long-necked lute. The rhythm is typically the 'aksak' meter.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in 'cemevleri' (Alevi meetinghouses) or during festivals like the Hacı Bektaş Veli Festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is one of the twelve services of the 'Cem' ritual. It symbolizes the unity of man with God and nature.
sections.notable_figures: Hacı Bektaş Veli is a central figure in the tradition.
sections.regional_variants: Forms include 'kirklar semahı' (sema of the forty) and 'turnalar semahı' (crane sema).
sections.lineage: Part of the broader Sufi tradition of 'Sama' (listening/remembrance), but distinct in its Alevi-Bektaşi practice.

claims.text: Semah is a set of mystical and aesthetic body movements in rhythmic harmony, constituting one of the twelve main services in Cem rituals.
The Semah is performed by both men and women side by side.
The music is determined by the aksak rhythm.
The right hand faces up and the left hand faces down.
The Semah was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List in 2010.

sections.origins_and_history: Moshing originated in the southern California hardcore punk scene, particularly Huntington Beach and Long Beach around 1978, evolving from the 1970s English pogo. Through the 1980s, it spread to Washington, D.C., Boston, and New York, where cross-pollination with heavy metal gave rise to the term 'mosh' via bands like Stormtroopers of Death and Anthrax. In the 1990s, grunge and festivals like Lollapalooza brought the mosh pit into mainstream consciousness, followed by later adoption in hip-hop and electronic dance music.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Participants push, slam, or run into each other inside a mosh pit. Variations include the Huntington Beach Strut (strutting in a circle while swinging arms), the Wall of Death (two halves of the audience charging at each other), circle pits (running counter-clockwise in a circle), and hardcore dancing (two-stepping, floorpunching, and windmilling).
sections.music_and_instruments: Performed to aggressive styles of live music featuring electric guitars, bass guitars, drums, and aggressive vocals, spanning punk rock, heavy metal, grunge, hardcore, hip-hop, and electronic dance music.
sections.costume_and_setting: Typically performed in concert venues, festivals, and underground music clubs. Participants generally wear casual street clothing, and sources note it is indispensable to avoid wearing glasses due to the high risk of eye injury.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Occurs during live music performances as a form of passionate fan feedback, release of energy, and underground cultural expression, though it has also been viewed by some as a manifestation of aggressive bullying.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Mike Marine (credited with the Huntington Beach Strut), H.R. of Bad Brains, Scott Ian and Billy Milano of Stormtroopers of Death, and artists associated with its mainstream spread like Billy Corgan and Travis Scott.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the Huntington Beach Strut in Southern California, Boston thrash and pig piles in Boston, New York hardcore style, psychobilly wrecking, and hip-hop pits which tend to feature jumping in unison rather than violent slamming.
sections.lineage: Directly descended from the 1970s English punk pogo, subsequently branching into regional hardcore styles, heavy metal moshing, grunge pits, and modern hip-hop raging.

sections.origins_and_history: The twist traces its stylistic lineage to African-American and African traditions, with historians Marshall and Jean Stearns noting that a pelvic dance motion called the twist came to America from the Congo during slavery. Early iterations appeared in blackface minstrelsy with Joel Walker Sweeney's 'Vine Twist' and the early 20th-century craze 'Mess Around'. Blues artists referenced the concept decades prior to the 1950s boom, including Bo Carter's 'Twist It Babe' in 1931 and Jelly Roll Morton's 'Winin' Boy Blues'. The modern dance took definitive shape among teenagers in the late 1950s, catalyzed by Hank Ballard's original song and catapulted to global fame by Chubby Checker's 1960 television debut.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The twist is performed standing with feet approximately shoulder-width apart. The hips, torso, and legs rotate on the balls of the feet as a single unit, with feet grinding back and forth on the floor as if putting out a cigarette. Knees are bent slightly, and arms are held out from the body, bent at the elbow. Hips swivel from side to side while upper body sways, with dancers maintaining a low posture and very little vertical motion, requiring no physical contact between partners.
sections.music_and_instruments: Driven by upbeat rock and roll instrumentation featuring electric guitars, drums, piano, and saxophone, alongside energetic vocal performances. Hit recordings featured driving backbeats and call-and-response structures designed to propel continuous physical movement.
sections.costume_and_setting: Danced in informal youth settings, discotheques, and television stages. Costumes reflected early 1960s casual wear, ranging from teenage skirts and trousers to sophisticated club attire at venues like New York's Peppermint Lounge.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Functioned as a spontaneous youth craze that bridged social divides, transforming rock music into a mass-market phenomenon while sparking generational debates over its suggestive pelvic motions.
sections.notable_figures: Chubby Checker, Hank Ballard, Dick Clark, Joey Dee, Bill Haley, Sam Cooke, Bo Diddley.
sections.regional_variants: Exported internationally, yielding localized versions such as Mexico's 'Spanish Twist' and 'Florida Twist' by Bill Haley, French yé-yé adaptations by Johnny Hallyday and Eddy Mitchell, and British pop versions.
sections.lineage: Influenced subsequent 1960s fad dances including the Jerk, the Pony, the Watusi, the Mashed Potato, the Monkey, and the Funky Chicken.

sections.origins_and_history: Developed from mid-19th-century prize walks on Southern US plantations, the cakewalk was exhibited at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia. It moved into minstrel shows and eventually Broadway, starring performers like Dora Dean and Charles E. Johnson, before becoming an international sensation in Paris in 1903.
sections.how_it_is_danced: A lively partnered vernacular jazz dance featuring processional walking, high-stepping kicks, struts, slides, and an erect upper body tilted backward, alternating with frantic jumps and turns.
sections.music_and_instruments: Notated in a 2/4 time signature with an oompah rhythm, incorporating syncopation, polyrhythms, and habanera rhythms. Historically played with banjos and violins, it heavily shaped the development of ragtime.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wore handed-down finery including top hats, swallow-tail coats, large bow ties, canes, and long ruffled hoop skirts. Settings ranged from plantation yards to rented halls with banked spectator tiers.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during Sunday gatherings and nighttime parties as a recreational pastime and a covert satire of white aristocratic European dances, with slaveholders awarding cakes to winning couples.
sections.notable_figures: Dora Dean, Charles E. Johnson, Tom Fletcher, Eugénie Fougère, Aida Overton Walker, Will Marion Cook.
sections.regional_variants: Spread from Florida across Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and New York, reaching international popularity in Paris and influencing early tango styles in Buenos Aires.
sections.lineage: Rooted in African American plantation culture, influenced by the ring shout, and serving as a direct precursor and sibling style to ragtime music.

sections.origins_and_history: The pogo emerged around 1976 during the early days of London's punk scene. Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious claimed to have invented the dance to mock non-punk attendees, while others attribute it to his leather poncho restricting movement or his frantic jumping while playing saxophone. It served as an anti-disco movement to counter mainstream rhythm.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers jump up and down while either remaining on the spot or moving around. The classic version involves keeping the torso stiff, arms rigid at the sides, and legs close together like a pogo stick. Variations allow for thrashing torsos, flailing arms, kicking legs, spinning in the air, and horizontal pushing.
sections.music_and_instruments: Associated primarily with punk rock, heavy metal, hardcore, and alternative rock genres. Instruments typically include electric guitars, bass guitars, drums, and occasional saxophones. The musical style is fast-paced and aggressive, designed to counter regular disco beats.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in underground music venues, clubs, and massive outdoor festivals (such as Monsters of Rock or large punk/metal gatherings). Attire reflects punk, underground, and counter-culture styles, historically including leather jackets, ponchos, and everyday street clothing.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed during live music performances of aggressive genres like punk and heavy metal. It serves as an expression of underground counter-culture, anti-establishment sentiment, and raw energy, underpinned by an unwritten code of community solidarity and safety for fallen dancers.
sections.notable_figures: Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols is widely credited with inventing or popularizing the dance. Other early figures associated with its lore include Shane MacGowan, Viv Albertine, and Glen Matlock. In Argentina, rock singer Indio Solari is renowned for fronting massive crowds during famous pogo events.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include slam dancing (slamming into others), moshing (pushing in a crowd without high vertical jumps), stage diving, slamming from the stage, wall of death (two halves of a crowd crashing together), and circle pits (running in a circle). Local names include mosh, tangana, olla, pateo, foso, mocha, and agite.
sections.lineage: The pogo is a direct precursor to modern moshing and slam dancing, sharing historical proximity with ska skanking and rockabilly traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: The origins of Seungmu are uncertain, with little extant evidence. Some theories link it to the monk Wonhyo or to the mocking of upper-class priests. Once prohibited during the Joseon dynasty, it was transformed into a folk dance by kisaengs and later refashioned into stage art by Han Sŏngjun in 1936.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed solo. It begins with the dancer crouched on the ground, slowly expanding their motion. The dancer uses long, white sleeves to create expressive shapes in the air. The performance involves eight rhythmic cycles that dictate changes in mood and footwork, moving from slow, heavy rhythms to faster, more complex drum-driven sequences.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by eight rhythmic cycles: yeombul, dodeuri, taryeong, jajin taryeong, gutgeori, dwit gutgeori, gujeong nori, and saesanjo. The 'bubgo' (drum) is the most important instrument, serving as a central element of the performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dancer wears a 'jangsam' (a robe with long, white sleeves) and a 'gokkal' (a white hood). The costume is described as radiant with elegant lines.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Seungmu is a form of art that communicates to the public. It symbolizes the birth of the universe, the four azimuths, the course of life, and human emotions like joy, wrath, and sorrow.
sections.notable_figures: Lee Mae Bang (deceased 2015), Kim Myo Seon, Kim Myung Ja, and Han Young-suk are noted as masters or master assistants of this tradition.
sections.regional_variants: The dance was improvised in variegated forms in different regions until the 1930s when various styles were archived and choreographed.
sections.lineage: The dance is a descendant of folk art traditions and shares commonalities with Buddhist ritual dances, though it is distinct from them.

claims.text: Seungmu is a Korean dance performed by Buddhist monks, designated as South Korea's important intangible cultural asset number 27 in 1969.
The dance was refashioned into stage art in 1936 by Han Sŏngjun.
The dance integrates eight rhythmic cycles: yeombul, dodeuri, taryeong, jajin taryeong, gutgeori, dwit gutgeori, gujeong nori, and saesanjo.
The dancer wears a robe (jangsam) with long sleeves and a white hood (gokkal).
The dance is considered a living tradition preserved by Human Cultural Treasures.

sections.origins_and_history: Investigations trace the siciliana back to 14th-century poetic-musical compositions inspired by Sicilian folk songs. It evolved through the Renaissance strambotto and 17th-century recitar cantando before codifying into Baroque instrumental and operatic forms. The earliest reference to the term regarding a dance appears in Tommaso Garzoni's 1599 work 'La piazza universale di tutte le professioni del mondo'.

sections.occasions_and_meaning: Evokes a pastoral, bucolic, and sentimental mood. In Baroque opera and Classical compositions, it was frequently used to portray grief, lamentation, and rustic scenes.

sections.regional_variants: Associated with Sicilian roots and Italian traditions, spreading across Europe into French (sicilienne) and German compositional practices.
sections.lineage: Derived from 14th-century Sicilian folk-inspired poetry and Renaissance strambotto, developing into a Baroque instrumental and vocal form utilized through the 20th century.

claims.text: The siciliana is a musical style or genre often included as a movement within larger pieces of music starting in the Baroque period.
It is in a slow 6/8 or 12/8 time with lilting rhythms, making it somewhat resemble a slow jig or tarantella, and is usually in a minor key.
Investigations by Ottavio Tiby demonstrate the definitive Sicilian roots of the siciliana, tracing it back to 14th-century poetic-musical compositions inspired by the island's folk songs.
La sicilienne est une danse traditionnelle vraisemblablement originaire de la Sicile, à caractère pastoral, bucolique et sentimental.

claims.text: Gainjeonmokdan is a Korean court dance called jeongjae, meaning beautiful people plucking peonies.
It was initiated and arranged by Crown Prince Hyomyeong in 1829 to please King Sunjo and was first recorded in the Mujajinjak uiqwe in 1828.
Peonies in a large vase are placed in the center of the stage while female dancers from two groups move around it, pick a peony one by one, and dance in a calm movement.
Changsa are verses of the accompanying song used for gainjeonmokdan.

sections.origins_and_history: The fouetté en tournant was introduced in the Grand Pas d'azione of the ballet Cinderella on December 17, 1893, with choreography by Lev Ivanov, Enrico Cecchetti, and Marius Petipa, and music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel. Pierina Legnani performed 32 consecutive fouettés without traveling, a feat reported by St. Petersburg Gazette critic Konstantin Skalkovski. Legnani repeated this in Swan Lake (1895), and Mathilde Kschesinskaya later achieved the same milestone.
sections.how_it_is_danced: A fouetté turn begins standing on one flat foot in plié with the knee bent. The working leg is extended and whipped to the side to create momentum, then pulled into a retiré or passé position while the supporting foot rises to relevé or en pointe. This creates the angular momentum needed for a rotation in place.
sections.music_and_instruments: The historic introduction of 32 consecutive fouettés in Cinderella featured music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel. The movement is subsequently incorporated into the grand pas and major ballets such as Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake.
sections.costume_and_setting: not described in sources
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performing 32 consecutive fouettés is considered a bravura demonstration of a ballerina's strength, stamina, and technique. It is a highly difficult feat that many dancers can execute on only one side, usually the right.

sections.lineage: A foundational virtuoso step of classical ballet within the classical-court tradition.

The working leg is extended and whipped around to the side and then pulled in to a passe or retiré position.

The 32 fouettés were introduced in the Grand Pas d'azione of Cinderella with music by Baron Boris Vietinghoff-Scheel.

sections.origins_and_history: The roots of the polska are traced to 17th-century Polish court influences interacting with indigenous Nordic musical structures and older triple-meter folk songs.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced primarily as a couple, featuring walking promenades, counter-clockwise upper-body turns (bakmes), and rapid clockwise rotations (pols) executed in triple time.
sections.music_and_instruments: Played on standard violins and the Hardanger fiddle, structured around repeating 32 or 64-measure phrases with variable rhythmic accents.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditionally performed in regional Nordic folk costumes within community halls, village squares, and mountain settlements.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed socially at community gatherings, weddings, and festivals across Sweden, Norway, and neighboring Nordic regions.
sections.notable_figures: Archivists and researchers such as those from Svenskt visarkiv and regional contributors who documented disappearing traditions in the mid-20th century.
sections.regional_variants: Includes Norwegian pols and springar, Swedish slängpolskas in Småland, and diverse community styles across Dalarna and Uppland.
sections.lineage: Descended from 17th-century European court dances and Nordic folk songs; gave rise to modern forms like the Swedish hambo.

claims.text: The polska is a family of music and dance forms shared across the Nordic countries.
The roots of the polska are traced back to 17th-century Polish court influences.
Norway's dances show the most consistent living tradition with unique local dances performed socially.
Swedish polska dance traditions came under severe pressure during industrialization.
La polska est une danse de couple à trois temps, originaire de Scandinavie.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is rooted in Swedish folk traditions, taking its name from the concept of throwing or flinging ("släng"). It spans regions from Östergötland and Värmland to northern Sweden, maintaining historical ties to Nordic dance families like the polska and related Norwegian forms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced either stationary in small groups or traveling counterclockwise around a room. Features distinct holds with outstretched crossed hands, close shoulder holds, hand-clap breaks, and per-measure rotational jumps.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is primarily in 3/4 time with sixteenth-note polska structures, where the first three beats have equal stress and length. Free variants may use 2/4 or 4/4 time.

sections.lineage: Part of the Swedish polska tradition, with structural similarities to Norwegian gangar and bonde dances.

claims.text: The Slängpolska is a Swedish folk dance whose name comes from the Swedish word for toss, throw, or chuck.
Slängpolskor are divided into two major types, with the first type featuring stationary dancing for two or four people focusing on holds.
A typical Type 1 slängpolska step consists of four steps over three beats: one long, two short, one long.
The second type involves couples moving counterclockwise around the room periphery at a high tempo with a tossing feeling and rotational jumps.
